caveats: Exact enumeration under a known assignment law and Monte Carlo reference draws have separate guarantees; exact sharp-null calibration requires no effect-increasing assumption.

The sampled guarantees require one fixed statistic applied to exchangeable values, with fresh iid assignment draws as a sufficient construction; they do not automatically cover statistics depending on a fixed or estimated reference bank.
The numerical sampled bounds use the printed strict cutoff; the archived weak cutoff is a different rule and has separate counterexamples.

The 256-unit level theorems assume the true sharp network model and a fixed symmetric binary network; they do not certify the reported empirical rejection frequencies or the application’s confidence rectangle.

Group-margin comparisons concern the simple regression with an intercept and own treatment, with both groups nonempty; additional network regressors can use alignment information beyond those margins.

The exposure and other finite witnesses are constructed examples; bank entries retain their multiplicities, conditional centering requires both treatment classes for each unit, and standardization requires positive sample standard deviation.

corrections.what: Against the printed contrast attributing additional joint-distribution information to simple SSR, the corrected result proves that both simple SSR and two-sided KS are unchanged when the two empirical group multisets, including multiplicities, are unchanged.

Against the printed description of the exposure transformation as normalizing raw sums, the corrected four-unit construction proves that neither the centered exposure nor its standardized version can be represented by an intercept, own treatment, and a multiple of the raw similarity sum.

In place of comparing the raw observed statistic with adjusted reference statistics as printed, using the adjusted outcomes at the observed assignment gives the same statistic law as the uniformity trial and a valid inclusive upper-tail test under a true additive hypothesis for any finite design.

The printed KS formula omits an absolute value; with both groups nonempty, the corrected two-sided statistic equals the supremum over real thresholds of the absolute ECDF difference, is invariant to exchanging labels, and lies in $[0,1]$.

The printed discussion identifies distributional divergence sensitivity with the directional effect-increasing property; the corrected statement proves that neither the two-sided nor the printed signed KS statistic has that property on the four-unit domain.

For exchangeable observed and reference statistics and $B\ge1$, replacing each raw tail proportion $C/B$ by the inclusive rank $(1+C)/(B+1)$ gives valid one-sided and capped doubled-minimum tests at every level in $[0,1]$, allowing ties.

key_results.what: For the paper’s multiplicative network model with nonnegative fixed weights and $\beta>0$, dividing generated outcomes by their assignment-specific multipliers recovers the same uniformity outcome vector for every assignment.

Under the true network model at $(\beta,\tau)=(2,1/2)$, a fixed symmetric binary network, and uniform assignment of 128 of 256 units, every statistic of adjusted outcomes and assignment gives exact inclusive upper-tail, lower-tail, and capped doubled-minimum tests with rejection probability at most $0.05$.

Under the same 256-unit sharp network model with fresh iid observed and reference assignments and one fixed statistic, the printed strict $0.05$ sampled two-tail rule has rejection probability at most $50/1001$ for 1000 references and $500/10001$ for 10000 references.

For fixed adjusted outcomes and fixed positive treatment and control group sizes, the lower-tail randomization probability of the simple within-group residual sum of squares equals the upper-tail probability of the absolute difference in means under any finite assignment law.

overview.overview: The work develops randomization tests under sharp hypotheses about direct effects and interference, using adjusted uniformity outcomes and regression residual statistics. The Lean development verifies the outcome mappings, exact finite-design level guarantees, and sampled-reference guarantees under explicit exchangeability or iid assumptions. Corrections distinguish group-margin information from network alignment, specify the test statistics and exposure transformation, and separate strict rejection cutoffs from the archived weak-cutoff rule.

text.body: The three Lean statements give the exact examples of P016-E004. Here $R(u,z)$ is the residual sum of squares from the regression of the adjusted outcomes $u$ on an intercept and the assignment $z$, which is the simple SSR statistic. The two-sided KS statistic is $D(u,z)=\max_i|F_1(u_i)-F_0(u_i)|$. The first statement takes $z=(1,1,0,0)$ with $u=(0,2,1,3)$ and with $u'=(0,2,3,1)$. It asserts that the covariance of the treated values with the control values in the listed order, with divisor $2$, is $1$ for $u$ and $-1$ for $u'$, while $R=4$ and $D=1/2$ for both. The other two statements take $u=(0,1,2,3)$ under complete randomization of two of the four units, and under the design that treats one unit in each of the blocks $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$. They list $R$ and $D$ at every assignment of each design. At the assignment $z$ that treats units 1 and 2, they assert that $\Pr\{R(u,Z)\le R(u,z)\}$ and $\Pr\{D(u,Z)\ge D(u,z)\}$ both equal $1/3$ under the first design and $1/2$ under the second. They assert also that the covariance of the two group means over the design is $-5/12$ under the first and $-1/2$ under the second. Each design is the list of its equally likely assignments, and all values are exact. The pairing in the first statement is an illustration, since the paper defines no pairing of treated with control units.

text.body: Ten Lean statements give the mathematical content of the correction P016-E004. Let $a$ be the fixed vector of adjusted outcomes, let $z$ be an assignment of $n\ge2$ units with $n_1>0$ treated and $n_0>0$ control units, and let $m_g$ be the mean of $a$ in group $g$. Two statements assert that the least squares fit of $a$ on an intercept and $z$ has the unique minimizer $(m_0,m_1-m_0)$, and that its residual sum of squares $R(a,z)=\sum_i(a_i-m_{z_i})^2$ satisfies $R(a,z)=T(a)-\frac{n_0n_1}{n}(m_1-m_0)^2,$ where $T(a)$ is the sum of squares of $a$ about the mean of all units. Two statements concern an assignment $w$ with as many treated units as $z$. They assert that $R(a,w)\le R(a,z)$ holds if and only if $|m_1(w)-m_0(w)|\ge|m_1(z)-m_0(z)|$. They assert also that, under every design on such assignments, the lower-tail probability of $R$ equals the upper-tail probability of the absolute difference in means. Three statements assert that $R$ is determined by the sizes and the first two moments of the two groups. They assert also that $R$ and the two-sided KS statistic each take the same value on any two data sets with the same multiset of treated values and the same multiset of control values. Another asserts that, under every design with fixed group sizes, $n_1m_1+n_0m_0$ is constant and $\operatorname{Cov}(m_1,m_0)=-(n_1/n_0)\operatorname{Var}(m_1)$, and that the two group ECDFs satisfy the same relations at every threshold. Two statements are examples on four units. In one, two outcome vectors with the same group values have SSR $0$ and SSR $4$ once degree is added to the regression; in the other, two assignments give the KS statistic $1/2$ with $R=4$ and with $R=5$. A design is a finite list of assignments with nonnegative probabilities that sum to one. The equivalence of the two tests is asserted for one adjusted vector and one pair of group sizes, as in the correction.

text.body: The five Lean statements give exact examples for P016-E006. For scores $s_i$, let $S_{ij}=1-|s_i-s_j|/2$ for $i\ne j$ and $S_{ii}=0$, and let $h_i(z)=(Sz)_i-\mu_{iz_i}$, where $\mu_{ia}$ is the mean of $(Sz')_i$ over the assignments $z'$ of a matched-pair design with $z'_i=a$. The first statement takes four units with scores $(-1,-1/2,1/2,1)$, the pairs $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$, and $z=(1,0,1,0)$. It asserts that $Sz=(1/4,5/4,1/4,3/4)$ and $h(z)=(1/8,1/8,-1/8,-1/8)$, and that no real $A$, $B$, $C$ satisfy $h_i(z)=A+Bz_i+C(Sz)_i$ for all $i$. It asserts the same with the sums of the distances $|s_i-s_j|$ to treated units in place of $(Sz)_i$. The fifth takes the six-unit example of P016-E006, with its vectors $Sz$ and $h(z)$. It asserts that $h(z)$ has neither the form $A+C\,Sz$ nor the form $A+Bz+C\,Sz$, and that for $y=(0,1,0,1,1,0)$ the residual sum of squares is $4/3$ on $(1,z,h)$ and $655/708$ on $(1,z,Sz)$. Two statements concern the first four rows of the application table of the replication files, with the decimals of the table read as exact rationals. With $x$ the raw exposure and $h$ the exposure after the subtraction, the determinant of the columns $(1,Z,x,h)$ is $-14030283848669586515272953541/10^{28}$, and no $A$, $B$, $C$ satisfy $h=A+BZ+Cx$ on these rows. The fourth takes the reference values $1,\ldots,1000$ and the two-sided $p$ value of the simulation code, twice the smaller tail proportion capped at $1$. At the observed value $25$ this $p$ value is exactly $1/20$, so that the rule $p\le.05$ rejects and the printed rule $p<.05$ does not. At $40$ the lower-tail proportion is at most $.05$ while the two-sided $p$ value exceeds $.05$, and at $980$ the reverse holds. In the constructed examples the means $\mu_{ia}$ are taken over all assignments of the matched-pair design, and in the application over 10,000 sampled assignments. The statements bear on the reading of the printed normalization as centring and scaling, and they assert nothing about Fig. 4 or the rectangle on p. 402.

text.body: Six Lean statements give properties of the corrected model of P016-E006. Let $S$ be a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal on $n\ge2$ units, and let a finite list of saved assignments contain each unit in both treatment states. Let $h_i(z)=(Sz)_i-z_i\mu_{i1}-(1-z_i)\mu_{i0}$ and $e_i(z)=(h_i(z)-\bar h(z))/s_h(z)$ be as in the correction, where $s_h(z)$ is the sample standard deviation across units. The first statement asserts that, if $y(z)=y^0+\beta_1z+\beta_2e(z)$ for every assignment $z$ of a design on which $s_h(z)>0$, then the adjusted outcome $y(z)-\beta_1z-\beta_2e(z)$ equals $y^0$ for every such $z$. The fourth asserts that, when $s_h(z)>0$, $e(z)$ has mean $0$ and sample variance $1$, and that the residual sum of squares on an intercept, $z$ and the exposure is the same with $h(z)$ as with $e(z)$. The sixth takes $S_{ij}=1-|s_i-s_j|/2$ with every score defined, $D_{ij}=|s_i-s_j|$, and saved assignments that all have $m$ treated units, as $z$ has. It asserts that $(Sz)_i=m-z_i-(Dz)_i/2$, that the centred exposures built from $S$ and from $D$ satisfy $h^S(z)=-h^D(z)/2$, and that $e^S(z)=-e^D(z)$ when $s_{h^D}(z)>0$. The fifth takes four units with scores $(-1,-1/2,1/2,1)$ in the pairs $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$, with the four assignments of the matched-pair design as the saved list. At $z=(1,0,1,0)$ it asserts that $s_h(z)>0$, and that neither $h(z)$ nor $e(z)$ has the form $A+Bz+C\,Sz$. The second and third concern the tail rules: for $B\ge1$ reference values the proportions that are at most and at least the observed value sum to at least $1$, and $p\le\alpha$ holds without $p<\alpha$ exactly when $p=\alpha$. The statements take every outcome as observed, and the application regression uses only the 67 legislators with observed outcomes. That neither the one-sided nor the two-sided rule implies the other appears only in a numerical example, which is among the statements for the printed description. The statements assert nothing about the level of the application’s test, whose reference assignments are drawn from the saved list.

text.body: The passage is an explanation and not a theorem, and the paper defines neither the joint distribution of treated and control outcomes nor their correlation. The Lean statement proves that the following situation is impossible: there are two data sets with the same multiset of treated values, the same multiset of control values and the same two-sided KS statistic, but different values of the simple SSR statistic. In words, the simple SSR statistic would use information that the two group distributions, and hence the KS statistic, do not carry. The two data sets are vectors of the same number $n\ge2$ of outcomes, each with an assignment, and both groups of the first assignment are nonempty. Equation (1) is read as the residual sum of squares on an intercept and the assignment, and the KS statistic is read with absolute values, as in P016-E002. This reading is one precise sense of the printed claim; it is supplied here and is not printed. A narrower statement is true: the randomization distribution of the SSR statistic reflects the dependence induced by the design. It holds equally for the KS statistic, and it belongs to the corrected passage of P016-E004.

text.body: The printed passage defines a model and a rejection rule. The three Lean statements say what follows from these definitions. In the first, $\Gamma$ is a distance matrix on $n\ge2$ units, $z$ is an assignment, and $g$ is any function such that the vector $g(\Gamma z)$ has sample variance $1$ across units. It asserts that, if $y_{\mathbf z}=y^0+\beta_1z+\beta_2g(\Gamma z)$, then $y_{\mathbf z}-\beta_1z-\beta_2g(\Gamma z)=y^0$. The third asserts the same for all assignments of a finite nonempty design at once. Under the true parameters, the adjusted outcome then does not depend on the assignment. The second restates the printed rule: a hypothesis is rejected exactly when $p<1/20$. The paper does not specify $g$ beyond unit variance, and the Lean statements leave it arbitrary. Two conventions are added: the variance has divisor $n-1$, and a distance matrix is nonnegative, symmetric and zero on the diagonal, and satisfies the triangle inequality. The identities do not depend on these conventions. The statements do not assert that the printed model is the model computed for Fig. 4; see P016-E006.

text.body: The three Lean statements give two examples for P016-E001, in which the comparison of step (4) as printed is applied to a true hypothesis. The statistic at the raw outcomes $Y$ is set against the randomization distribution of the statistic at the adjusted outcomes $u=Y-\tau_0Z$. The first two statements take four units with outcomes $(0,1,2,3)$ without treatment, under complete randomization of two units. The effect is additive with $\tau=\tau_0=10$, and the statistic is the difference in group means. They assert that the statistic at $u$ takes the values $-2,-1,0,0,1,2$ over the six assignments and the statistic at $Y$ the values $8,9,10,10,11,12$. They assert further that, under every assignment, no reference value is as large as the raw statistic, in absolute value or in the upper tail. The printed comparison then rejects the true hypothesis with probability one at every level $\alpha>0$. The third statement takes eight units with outcomes $0,\ldots,7$, under complete randomization of four units, with $\tau=\tau_0=-100$. The statistic is the KS statistic, in the signed form of footnote 3 and in the two-sided form. The statement asserts that both forms equal $1$ at the raw outcomes under every assignment, and that the reference probabilities of a value at least $1$ are $1/70$ and $1/35$. It asserts that the printed comparison rejects the true hypothesis with probability one, against $1/70$ and $1/35$ when the adjusted outcomes are used on both sides. In this example rejection means $p<1/20$, where $p$ is the exact upper-tail probability over the equally likely assignments. The examples concern the literal recipe and not the method that the paper intends.

text.body: Three Lean statements give the content of the corrected step of P016-E001. Let $y_{\cdot,0}$ be the outcomes without treatment, let the effect be additive with parameter $\tau$, so that $Y_i=y_{i,0}+\tau Z_i$, and let $u_i(\tau_0)=Y_i-\tau_0Z_i$. The first statement asserts that $u_i(\tau_0)=y_{i,0}+(\tau-\tau_0)Z_i$, and hence that $u(\tau)=y_{\cdot,0}$ under every assignment. The second takes any design on finitely many assignments, any statistic $\mathcal T$ and any $\alpha\in[0,1]$, with $\tau_0=\tau$. It asserts that the observed statistic $\mathcal T(u,Z)$ has the distribution of $\mathcal T(y_{\cdot,0},Z')$, where $Z'$ follows the design, and that the $p$ value $p=\Pr_{Z'}\{\mathcal T(u,Z')\ge\mathcal T(u,Z)\}$ satisfies $\Pr\{p\le\alpha\}\le\alpha$. The third asserts that, for the difference in group means with both groups nonempty, $\mathcal T(Y,z)=\mathcal T(u(\tau_0),z)+\tau_0$, so that the printed and the corrected statistic agree if and only if $\tau_0=0$. The design is a finite set of labelled outcomes of the randomization, with nonnegative probabilities that sum to one. Each label is mapped to an assignment, and the statistic may depend on the label. Only the upper-tail $p$ value is treated here. The lower-tail and two-sided $p$ values are covered by the statements on validity under a sharp null hypothesis that accompany P016-E005.

text.body: The three Lean statements give the examples of P016-E002, one for each display. For footnote 3, the first takes $u=(0,1,2,3)$ and $z=(0,0,1,1)$, where $F_1-F_0$ takes the values $-1/2,-1,-1/2,0$ at the four sample points. It asserts that the maximum as printed is $0$ and the maximum of the absolute values is $1$, and that both are $1$ when the two groups are exchanged. For equation (1), the second takes $u=(0,1,2,3)$ under complete randomization of two of the four units. The sum of squares about the mean of all units is $5$ and does not depend on the assignment. The statement asserts that the lower-tail and upper-tail $p$ values of this quantity at the assignment that treats units 1 and 2 are $1$. It asserts also that the lower-tail $p$ value of the residual sum of squares on an intercept and $z$ is $1/3$ there. For equation (2), the third takes six units whose only edge joins units 1 and 2, with $z=(1,0,1,0,1,0)$ and $u=(1,\ldots,1)$. It asserts that the residual sum of squares of the least squares fit is $0$ on the columns $(1,z_i,(z^TS)_i,(1^TS)_i)$ and $2$ on the three listed columns without the constant. The second example depends on reading the undefined mean of equation (1) as the mean over all units. The third depends on reading the printed list of columns as complete. In the Lean statements each maximum is taken together with $0$, which changes nothing when both groups are nonempty. The missing row index of equation (2) has no statement of its own.
text.headline: A counterexample to each of footnote 3, equation (1) and equation (2), as printed
text.location: Footnote 3, p. 396 (PDF p. 2); equation (1), p. 397 (PDF p. 3); equation (2) and the sentence before it, p. 399 (PDF p. 5)

text.body: Four Lean statements give the facts that make the corrected displays of P016-E002 well defined. Let $u$ be the adjusted outcomes and $z$ an assignment with both groups nonempty. For equation (1), the fourth asserts that $\sum_i(u_i-\bar u_{z_i})^2$ is the minimum of $\sum_i(u_i-a-bz_i)^2$ over real $a$ and $b$, attained only at $a=\bar u_0$ and $b=\bar u_1-\bar u_0$. For equation (2), the first asserts that, for every real matrix $X$ with $n$ rows, the minimum of $\|u-Xb\|_2^2$ over $b$ is attained and that all minimizers give the same fitted vector $Xb$. No condition on the rank of $X$ is imposed. For footnote 3, the second asserts that $\max_{1\le i\le n}|F_1(u_i)-F_0(u_i)|=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|F_1(t)-F_0(t)|,$ ties included, and that this statistic is unchanged when the two groups are exchanged and lies in $[0,1]$. The third asserts that, for a symmetric adjacency matrix $S$ with entries $0$ and $1$, $(z^TS)_i=\sum_jS_{ij}z_j$ and $(1^TS)_i=\sum_jS_{ij}$. The fourth statement requires $n\ge2$. The third assumes symmetry and binary entries, and requires both assignment groups to be nonempty. It imposes no zero-diagonal condition: a diagonal entry, when present, contributes once to each corresponding sum. For a network without self-links, the diagonal is zero and these sums count treated neighbours and degree.

text.body: The two Lean statements give examples for P016-E005. A statistic $T(y,z)$ is effect increasing if, at a fixed assignment $z$, raising treated responses and lowering control responses cannot decrease it. The paper does not define the term, and this is the definition used in the correction. The first statement fixes $z=(1,1,0,0)$. It asserts that from $y=(0,1,2,3)$ to $y'=(2,3,2,3)$ no treated response falls and no control response rises. It asserts also that the two-sided KS statistic $\max_i|F_1(y_i)-F_0(y_i)|$ falls from $1$ to $0$, as does the signed maximum printed in footnote 3. It asserts further that from $(0,1,4,5)$ to $(2,3,2,3)$ every treated response rises strictly and every control response falls strictly, and that the KS statistic of $(0,1,4,5)$ is $1$. The second statement asserts that the residual sum of squares on an intercept and $z$ is $4$ at $(0,2,0,2)$, $5/2$ when the first treated response is raised to $1$, and $13/2$ when instead the second is raised to $3$. These statements give numerical values and inequalities between the responses. That the KS statistic is not effect increasing is asserted by a separate statement, among those for the corrected passage. The statements do not concern the validity of the test or the content of the propositions cited from Rosenbaum (2002).
text.headline: A counterexample to the identification of the quoted property with “effect increasing”, as printed
text.location: pp. 396–397 (PDF pp. 2–3), the quotation that runs from the last line of p. 396 to the first lines of p. 397, and the sentence after it

text.body: Seven Lean statements give the content of the corrected sentences of P016-E005. A statistic $T(y,z)$ is called effect increasing if $T(y',z)\ge T(y,z)$ whenever $y'_i\ge y_i$ for the treated units of $z$ and $y'_i\le y_i$ for its control units. The sixth statement asserts that the difference in group means has this property at every assignment with both groups nonempty. The seventh asserts that, on four units, neither the two-sided KS statistic nor the signed maximum of footnote 3 has it. The first three statements give validity for an arbitrary statistic. Let $\Omega$ be a finite set of assignments with probabilities $q(z)>0$ that sum to one, and let $s$ be any real function on $\Omega$. Let $p_U(z)=\sum_{w:s(w)\ge s(z)}q(w)$, $p_L(z)=\sum_{w:s(w)\le s(z)}q(w)$ and $p_2=\min\{1,2\min(p_U,p_L)\}$. They assert that, for every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, $\Pr\{p_U(Z)\le\alpha\}\le\alpha,\qquad \Pr\{p_L(Z)\le\alpha\}\le\alpha,\qquad \Pr\{p_2(Z)\le\alpha\}\le\alpha .$ The fourth and fifth statements give the four-unit example, $y^0=(0,1,2,3)$ with two of four units treated and the two-sided KS statistic. In it $p_U=1/3,1,1,1,1,1/3$ over the six assignments, and $\Pr\{p_U(Z)\le\alpha\}$ is $0$ for $\alpha<1/3$, $1/3$ for $1/3\le\alpha<1$ and $1$ for $\alpha=1$. Under a sharp null hypothesis of no effect the outcomes are the same under every assignment, so that the statistic is a function $s$ of the assignment alone. Unbiasedness against alternatives is not treated.
text.headline: The two sentences after the quotation in Section 1, as corrected: the effect increasing property, and validity under a sharp null hypothesis for any statistic
text.location: p. 397 (PDF p. 3), first paragraph, second and third sentences

text.body: The five Lean statements concern the rule of the simulation code described in P016-E008, and not the printed rule $p<.05$. With $B\ge1$ sampled reference statistics, of which $L$ are at most and $U$ are at least the observed statistic, that rule sets $p_{\mathrm{raw}}=\min\{1,2\min(L,U)/B\}$ and rejects when $p_{\mathrm{raw}}\le\alpha$. The first statement takes an observed statistic and $B$ reference statistics that are exchangeable and almost surely distinct, with $0\le\alpha<1$, $c=\lfloor\alpha B/2\rfloor$ and $2c<B$. It asserts that the number of reference statistics below the observed one is uniform on $\{0,\ldots,B\}$, and that $\Pr\{p_{\mathrm{raw}}\le\alpha\}=2(c+1)/(B+1)$. The other statements concern sixteen units with fixed outcomes $2^i$ for $i=0,\ldots,15$, eight of them treated, and the residual sum of squares on an intercept and $z$ as the statistic. One gives its residual sum of squares, and another asserts that the design has $12870$ assignments and that the statistic takes $M=6435$ distinct values, two assignments sharing a value exactly when they are equal or complementary. A fourth takes the observed assignment and the $B$ reference assignments as independent uniform draws from this design. For integers $B\ge1$ and $c\ge0$ with $2c<B$, it asserts that the probability that $L\le c$ or $U\le c$ is $S_B(c)=\frac{2}{M}\sum_{r=1}^{M}\sum_{k=0}^{c}\binom{B}{k}\Bigl(\frac{r}{M}\Bigr)^{k}\Bigl(\frac{M-r}{M}\Bigr)^{B-k},$ and that $2(c+1)/(B+1)-2/M\le S_B(c)\le2(c+1)/(B+1)$ for every integer $0\le c<B$. For $B=1000$ and $B=10{,}000$ it asserts that the rule $p_{\mathrm{raw}}\le1/20$ rejects with probability $S_B(B/40)>1/20$ and the rule $p_{\mathrm{raw}}<1/20$ with probability $S_B(B/40-1)<1/20$. For every $B\ge1$ it asserts that $\Pr\{p_{\mathrm{raw}}=0\}=S_B(0)>0$. The fifth statement is the arithmetic $52/1001=4/77>1/20$, $502/10001>1/20$ and $4/77-2/6435=2326/45045>1/20$. These exact sums and inequalities establish the excess above the nominal level in this example; they do not concern the simulation of 256 units in the note.
text.headline: A counterexample to level $.05$ for the simulated permutation tests of Section 2.2 as the replication code implements them
text.location: p. 400 (PDF p. 6), Section 2.2, first and second paragraphs; p. 397 (PDF p. 3), the parenthesis on validity; the rule is in the simulation scripts of the replication files

text.body: Eight Lean statements give the content of the correction P016-E008. For $B\ge1$, let $T_0$ be the observed statistic and $T_1,\ldots,T_B$ the reference statistics. Suppose that their joint distribution is unchanged by every permutation of the $B+1$ indices; ties are allowed. Let $L$ and $U$ be the numbers of reference statistics that are at most and at least $T_0$, and let $p_{\mathrm{raw}}=\min\{1,2\min(L,U)/B\}$. The first statement asserts that $\Pr\{L\le c\}\le(c+1)/(B+1)$ and $\Pr\{U\le c\}\le(c+1)/(B+1)$ for every integer $0\le c\le B$. The second asserts, for the printed rule and every $0<\alpha<1$, that $\Pr\{p_{\mathrm{raw}}<\alpha\}\le\frac{2\lceil\alpha B/2\rceil}{B+1}.$ A companion statement evaluates this bound at $\alpha=1/20$: it is $50/1001$ for $B=1000$ and $500/10001$ for $B=10{,}000$, both below $1/20$. The third takes $p_L^+=(1+L)/(B+1)$, $p_U^+=(1+U)/(B+1)$ and $p_2^+=\min\{1,2\min(p_L^+,p_U^+)\}$. It asserts that $\Pr\{p_L^+\le\alpha\}\le\lfloor\alpha(B+1)\rfloor/(B+1)\le\alpha$, likewise for $p_U^+$, and that $\Pr\{p_2^+\le\alpha\}\le\alpha$, for every $\alpha\in[0,1]$. A further statement asserts that the exchangeability holds when one fixed statistic is applied to independent draws from one design on finitely many assignments. For exact tail probabilities, the three statements on validity under a sharp null hypothesis that accompany P016-E005 serve again. The statements do not cover the application, whose reference assignments are drawn from a fixed saved set.

text.body: The three Lean statements give small examples for the mathematical parts of items 1 to 3 of P016-E011. For the sentence on p. 398, the first takes $Y=(9,11,10,12)$ and $Z=(0,0,1,1)$. It asserts that the adjusted outcomes are $(9,11,19/2,23/2)$ under the additive hypothesis $\tau_0=1/2$ and $(9,11,5,6)$ under the multiplicative hypothesis $\tau_0=2$. It asserts also that the ECDF of the treated group at the threshold $6$ is $0$ under the first hypothesis and $1$ under the second. The control values are the same under both hypotheses, and the treated values differ. For footnote 3, the second asserts that the ECDF of the sample $(1,3)$ is $1/2$ at the argument $2$ and $1$ at the sample point $3$. For p. 400, the third asserts that a pair $(\tau,\beta)$ satisfies $\tau=\tau_0$ and $\beta=\tau_0$ for some $\tau_0$ exactly when $\beta=\tau$, and that the truth $(\tau,\beta)=(1/2,2)$ satisfies them for no $\tau_0$. The multiplicative adjustment $Y_i/(1+Z_i(\tau_0-1))$ is not printed; it is the inverse of the multiplicative model of p. 397. The other items of the correction, on the chamber, the references and the misprinted words, are not mathematical and have no Lean statement.
text.headline: A counterexample to each of three local statements, as printed: “control group distribution”, p. 398; “at or below $x_i$”, footnote 3; and “$\tau=\tau_0$, $\beta=\tau_0$”, p. 400

text.body: Four Lean statements give the content of the mathematical parts of items 1 to 3 of the correction P016-E011. Let $u_i(\tau_0)=Y_i-Z_i\tau_0$ be the additive adjustment, and let $v_i(\tau_0)=Y_i/(1+Z_i(\tau_0-1))$, with $\tau_0\ne0$, be the multiplicative one. The first statement asserts that $u_i(\tau_0)=v_i(\tau_0)=Y_i$ for a control unit. For a treated unit it asserts that $u_i(\tau_0)=Y_i-\tau_0$ and $v_i(\tau_0)=Y_i/\tau_0$, and that these differ for different values of $\tau_0$, in the case of $v_i$ when $Y_i\ne0$. The second asserts that the ECDF of the control group after either adjustment equals, at every threshold, the ECDF of the observed control outcomes. The third asserts that $F(x)=(1/n)\sum_iI(x_i\le x)$ equals $\#\{i:x_i\le x\}/n$ for every real $x$, the proportion of the sample at or below the argument. The fourth asserts that the stated truth $(\tau,\beta)=(1/2,2)$ belongs to the family $\tau=\tau_0$, $\beta=\beta_0$ with two free parameters, and to the printed family $\tau=\tau_0$, $\beta=\tau_0$ for no $\tau_0$. The first two statements hold for every number of units and every assignment. The corrections to the chamber, the references and the misprinted words have no Lean statement.

text.body: Two Lean statements concern the corrected comparison of P016-N002, in which both means are means of the adjusted outcome $u_i=Y_i-Z_i\tau$. The symbol $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=1}$ of the printed sentence is not defined in the paper. The first statement reads it as the potential outcome under treatment that the hypothesis implies, $u_i+\tau$, and takes any assignment with both groups nonempty. It asserts that $u_i+\tau=Y_i$ for every treated unit, and that the printed comparison then equals $\overline{(u+\tau)}_{Z=1}-\bar u_{Z=0}=(\bar u_{Z=1}-\bar u_{Z=0})+\tau=\bar Y_{Z=1}-\bar Y_{Z=0},$ the raw difference in means, in which the hypothesized $\tau$ does not appear. The second statement is the instance $u=(0,1,2,3)$, $\tau=10$ and $Z=(0,0,1,1)$, where the corrected comparison is $2$ and the printed one is $12$. The reading of the undefined symbol is a literal one, used to state what the printed term would compare. It is not the reading that the context suggests. An undefined term is not a false statement, so these statements illustrate the ambiguity rather than refute a defined proposition.

text.body: The Lean statement gives the exact example of P016-N003 with all 256 units. The 128 control outcomes are 64 nines and 64 elevens, and the 128 treated outcomes are one $8$, 63 nines, 63 elevens and one $12$. The additive parameter is $t=34/99$ and the multiplicative parameter is $a=1+t/8=413/396$. The statement asserts that both groups have mean $10$ and that the variance of the 256 outcomes, with divisor $256$, is $131/128$. It asserts that the absolute difference between the outcomes generated by the two models is $0$ for every control unit and for the treated unit with outcome $8$, and is nonzero for the other 127 treated units. It asserts that the median of the 256 differences, the average of the 128th and the 129th smallest, is $0$. It asserts further that the multiplicative model raises the treated mean by $85/198=5t/4$, against $t$ for the additive model. The multiplicative adjustment lowers the treated mean by $170/413$, against $t$ for the additive adjustment, and the ratio of the two is $495/413>1$. The median is taken from the sorted list of all 256 differences. The population is constructed on the design and the outcome scale of the note and is not its simulated data. The statement asserts nothing about the power values of Fig. 2.

text.body: Six Lean statements give the mathematical content of the mapping that the note uses to test a sharp hypothesis. The first is the identity of step (1): if $Y_i=Z_iy_{i,Z_i=1}+(1-Z_i)y_{i,Z_i=0}$ and $y_{i,Z_i=1}=y_{i,Z_i=0}+\tau$, then $y_{i,Z_i=0}=Y_i-Z_i\tau$. The sixth asserts that adjusting outcomes generated with effect $\tau$ by $\tau_0$ gives $y_{i,Z_i=0}+(\tau-\tau_0)Z_i$, which is $y_{i,Z_i=0}$ under every assignment when $\tau_0=\tau$. The other four concern equation (3), read componentwise as $\mathcal H(\mathbf y_{\mathbf z},\mathbf w,\beta,\tau)_i=\{c_i(w)/c_i(z)\}\,y_{\mathbf z,i}$ with $c_i(v)=\beta+(1-v_i)(1-\beta)\exp\bigl(-\tau^2(v^TS)_i\bigr),\qquad (v^TS)_i=\sum_jv_jS_{ji}.$ For a matrix $S$ with nonnegative entries, $\beta>0$ and real $\tau$, they assert that $c_i(v)>0$, and that $c_i(\mathbf 0)=1$, so that the outcome with no unit treated implied by the model is $y_{\mathbf z,i}/c_i(z)$. They assert that the map from $\mathbf z$ to $\mathbf z$ is the identity, and that the map from $\mathbf z$ to $\mathbf w$ followed by the map from $\mathbf w$ to $\mathbf w'$ is the map from $\mathbf z$ to $\mathbf w'$. They assert finally that, if $y_{\mathbf z,i}=c_i(z)\,y_{\mathbf 0,i}$ for all $z$ and $i$, then $y_{\mathbf z,i}/c_i(z)=y_{\mathbf 0,i}$ for every $z$. The paper prints the identity for the additive model only. The properties of equation (3) are used in the note and not stated there. The paper gives no domain for $\beta$, and the condition $\beta>0$ is added so that the denominator of (3) cannot vanish. In these statements $S$ need not be binary or symmetric, which is broader than the adjacency matrix of the paper. The comparison of the statistic with its randomization distribution has its own Lean statements.
text.headline: Steps (1)–(2) of the testing procedure and equation (3): the mapping from observed outcomes to the outcomes with no unit treated

text.body: Two Lean statements give the level bound in the setting of Section 2.2. The network on the 256 units is a symmetric adjacency matrix $S$ with entries $0$ and $1$, and the $\binom{256}{128}$ assignments with 128 treated units are equally likely. The outcomes follow equation (3) with the true parameters $\beta=2$ and $\tau=1/2$. The test statistic is any function $T(u,z)$ of the adjusted outcomes and the assignment, which covers the six statistics of Fig. 3 without stating them one by one. The first statement asserts that the adjusted outcomes computed with the true parameters are the same under every assignment. It asserts further that, when the $p$ value is the exact upper-tail probability, the exact lower-tail probability, or twice the smaller of the two capped at $1$, $\Pr\{p\le.05\}\le.05\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Pr\{p<.05\}\le.05 .$ The second takes the observed assignment and $B$ reference assignments as independent draws from the design. The test uses $p_{\mathrm{raw}}=\min\{1,2\min(L,U)/B\}$, where $L$ and $U$ count the reference statistics that are at most and at least the observed one. It asserts that the printed rule $p_{\mathrm{raw}}<.05$ rejects the true hypothesis with probability at most $50/1001$ for $B=1000$ and at most $500/10001$ for $B=10{,}000$, both below $.05$. The paper prints no formula for the $p$ value, and these forms are supplied. The reported rejection rates of about 4% and 2% are simulation results and are not part of the statements. Neither is the rule $p\le.05$ of the simulation code, which is the subject of P016-E008.
